title: Shortness of Breath
hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an older man with history of prior myocardial infarction and hypertension on lisinopril who presents with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Exam reveals JVD, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles, and expiratory wheezing. CXR shows pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Echo confirms reduced ejection fraction — systolic dysfunction. BNP is elevated. The most common cause of systolic HF is ischemic heart disease. NYHA Class III-IV (symptoms with minimal activity). Treatment: IV loop diuretic (furosemide) for volume overload, continue ACEI, add nitroglycerin for afterload reduction. Once acute exacerbation resolves and patient is euvolemic, start beta-blocker (carvedilol preferred per COMET trial — 17% survival benefit over metoprolol, though bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate also accepted). Digoxin for symptom control if needed. No stress tests until recovered. Admit to inpatient unit. Discharge: low-sodium diet, smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, pneumococcal and zoster vaccines, Tdap.
chief_complaint: Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, LE edema

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
stacks.finding: Dyspnea + cardiac history — S3 gallop, JVD.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine
stacks.finding: Pitting edema — hallmark of R-sided HF.

stacks.label: TSH
stacks.finding: Thyroid pathology associated with arrhythmias precipitating HF.

stacks.label: Cardiac troponin
stacks.finding: Superimposed ischemia/infarction is common cause of HF exacerbation.

stacks.label: Chest X-ray
stacks.finding: Pulmonary edema + cardiomegaly. Rule out other causes of dyspnea.

stacks.label: Echocardiography
stacks.finding: Confirms CHF — reduced ejection fraction (systolic dysfunction).

stacks.label: Stress test / Stress echo
stacks.finding: NO stress tests until patient recovers from acute HF exacerbation.

stacks.label: Furosemide (Lasix) / Bumetanide / Torsemide
stacks.finding: Volume overloaded — loop diuretic for rapid symptom improvement.

stacks.label: Digoxin
stacks.finding: Helps symptoms, not outcomes. For moderate-severe CHF (NYHA III-IV) as adjunct.

stacks.label: Nitroglycerin
stacks.finding: Dilates coronary arteries — reduces afterload and improves coronary flow.

stacks.label: Beta-blocker (Carvedilol / Metoprolol / Bisoprolol)
stacks.finding: Start after diuresis, prior to discharge. Carvedilol preferred (COMET trial: 17% survival benefit over metoprolol). All 3 accepted.

physical_exam.cardiovascular: S3 gallop. JVD present. Prior MI history.
physical_exam.respiratory: Pulmonary crackles (rales), expiratory wheezing — pulmonary edema.

decoys.label: Stress test during acute exacerbation
decoys.reason_wrong: Stress tests contraindicated until acute CHF exacerbation resolves. Risk of decompensation.

decoys.label: Beta-blocker BEFORE diuresis
decoys.reason_wrong: Beta-blocker should be started after patient is euvolemic (post-diuresis), before discharge. Starting during acute volume overload can worsen hemodynamics.

teach_me_steps.order: Clinical diagnosis: JVD + S3 + crackles + edema
teach_me_steps.reasoning: Systolic HF = reduced EF. Most common cause: ischemic heart disease. BNP elevated, CXR shows pulmonary edema, echo confirms.
IV furosemide rapidly improves symptoms. Monitor I/Os. Once euvolemic → transition to PO.
COMET trial: carvedilol 17% survival benefit. Start before discharge after acute exacerbation resolves. Continue ACEI (lisinopril).

case_summary: Systolic CHF exacerbation (NYHA III-IV). Prior MI + HTN. IV Lasix → NTG → continue lisinopril → add carvedilol before discharge. Admit to inpatient. Lifestyle: low Na, smoking cessation, vaccines.
